newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam rails against human rights condemnation.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam rails against human rights condemnation.

text.p: Vietnam has reacted angrily to a critical report by the European Parliament on the communist country's human rights record, saying no one had the right to interfere in the internal affairs of a nation.

"The resolution of the European Parliament on so-called human rights violations in Vietnam is false and does not reflect the real situation in Vietnam..." the Foreign Ministry said in a statement sent to Reuters late on Saturday.
The European Parliament's resolution, issued last week, condemned rights violations committed by the government and called on Hanoi to release all political and religious prisoners.
It said the government continued to restrict civil liberties and violate human rights by significantly restricting freedom of speech, the media, assembly, association and religion.

The resolution also noted that although Vietnam's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, Hanoi was still pursuing "a policy of religious persecution", in particular against the Unified Buddhist Church of Vietnam (UBCV) and the Catholic Church.
It deplored the fact that all dignitaries of the now-outlawed UBCV had been imprisoned in "inhuman conditions".
The Foreign Ministry said that no country or international organisation had the right to interfere in the internal affairs of other nations.

It added that the reolution was not in keeping with a principle agreed between Vietnam and the European Union to respect freedom and sovereignty and not to interfere in each other's domestic affairs, which -- it warned -- does not benefit the development of cooperation between the two sides.
Vietnam signed a framework cooperation agreement with the EU in July 1995 which covered trade, investment promotion, the opening of markets, human rights and refugees.
The European Parliament approved the agreement in February 1996, but insisted that the human rights clause in the accord should not just be empty words.
A U.S. State Department issued a report earlier this year which described Hanoi's record on upholding freedoms as poor.

It referred to reports that some prisons used forced labour for commercial ventures, quoted estimates that Vietnam was holding between 70 and 1,000 political prisoners and criticised the behaviour of members of the powerful internal security agency.
Vietnam dismissed that report and countered by highlighting racial problems and violence in the United States and accusing Washington of years of warmongering at home and abroad.

Vietnam habitually rebukes overseas critics of its human rights record. Communist Party officials say that rights issues are being used as a pretext by forces intent on subverting the country's political regime.
